outputs.L1:
**I. — THE FIRST FUNERAL**

*(The first corpse I saw lay upon the German wires, and could not be buried)*

The whole field reeked so foully;
We smelt the poor dog first:
His swollen belly, ghastly,
Looked fit as though to burst.

His fur was all dishevelled;
He hadn't any eyes.
It happened on Good Friday,
And there were swarms of flies.

And then I felt the coldest
I'd ever felt, and sick;
But Rose, being the eldest,
Dared prod him with her stick.

He felt so soft and horrid:
The flies buzzed round his head
And settled on his forehead;
Rose whispered: "That dog's dead.

"We bury all dead people,
When they're quite truly dead,
By churches with a steeple:
Let's bury this," Rose said.

"And let us wreathe it round with mint
To veil the wretched smell."
I went to seek, and found it—
Great tufts, beside the well.

We eased him through the clover
Down in a hole, and then
We cast brown earth right over
And said: "Poor dog, Amen!"

---

**A note:** This is Robert Graves's poem "The First Funeral." I've gently refined the diction and smoothed the rhythm while preserving the rhyme scheme, the narrative, and the childlike voice. Because this is an established literary work, you may prefer to retain the original wording exactly—do let me know if you'd like a lighter touch or a return to the source text.

I. – THE FIRST FUNERAL
(The very first dead body I ever saw was tangled in the German wires, where no one could bury it)

A dreadful stench filled all the ground;
The wretched dog was what we sensed—
Its awful bloated stomach round
Seemed ready any moment to burst.

Its coat was tangled, matted, rough;
Where eyes should be, there was nothing there.
This came to pass on Good Friday's morn,
And swarms of flies were everywhere.

A chill then gripped me, worse than ever,
And nausea rose within my chest,
But Rose, since she's the eldest one,
Was brave enough to prod its breast.

He felt so soft, so sickening too:
The flies hummed all about his crown
And settled down upon his brow:
Rose murmured low: 'That dog's not around.'

'We give dead folk a proper grave,
Once they are truly, wholly dead,
By churches where the steeples rise:
Let's bury this one here,' Rose said.

'And let us circle it with mint
To mask the foul and rotten smell.'
I went to search and came upon it—
Great heaps of it beside the well.

We nudged him past the clover through
And down into a pit, and then
We heaped the dark brown soil on top
And spoke: 'Poor dog, Amen!'

# The Dead Dog

We found it in the field one afternoon, though at first we did not see it at all. It was the smell that reached us first—a thick, horrid stench that seemed to hang in the warm air and grow stronger with every step we took. Following it like a trail, we came upon the source: a dead dog lying in the long grass, its belly swollen grotesquely against the sky.

I shall never forget that sight. The poor creature was in an advanced state of decay, its body crawling and shifting with a black mass of flies that rose and settled in restless clouds. The horror of it went straight through me. Despite the sunshine, a cold shiver ran down my spine, and my stomach turned over so that I thought I might be sick right there in the field.

The rest of us stood frozen, none daring to move closer, but Rose—being the oldest among us—took charge as she always did. With a courage the rest of us lacked, she stepped forward, holding out her stick, and gave the corpse a tentative poke. The body did not stir. She poked again, harder this time, then straightened up and announced with grave certainty that the dog was quite dead.

The question then arose of what should be done. It was Rose again who reasoned it out. We knew, all of us, that when people died they were buried in the ground around the church, laid to rest beneath the earth. Surely, we decided, a dog deserved no less. And so it was settled: we would bury the dog ourselves.

First we set about gathering handfuls of wild mint from the edges of the field, crushing the leaves and heaping them over and around the body to smother that terrible smell. Then, working together, we dug a hole in the soft ground and, as gently as we could manage, laid the poor creature down into it. We filled the grave with the rich brown earth until nothing remained to be seen. And when it was done, we stood in a solemn little circle and spoke the only words that seemed fitting.

"Poor dog," we said. "Amen."
outputs.L4:
# The Burial

The epigraph sits above the poem like a shadow—those few words about a corpse left hanging on the German wires, unburied, exposed to weather and time. It colors everything that follows, though we children knew nothing of such distant horrors then. We knew only the field, the summer, and the thing we found lying in the tall grass.

It was Rose who saw it first. Being the eldest, she was always the one who saw things first, who decided what we would do and how we would do it. The dog lay half-hidden where the grass grew thickest, and at first we did not understand what we were looking at. Then the smell reached us—sweet and terrible, a smell I had no name for but would never afterward forget. The younger ones drew back. I remember wanting to run, but Rose stood very still, studying it the way she studied everything, her face grave and thoughtful.

The animal had been dead some while. Its coat had loosened; the shape of it had begun to sink into itself, to return to the earth in ways I did not have the words to describe but understood, in some wordless way, all the same. Flies moved over it in the heavy afternoon light. One of the little ones began to cry, and Rose told them to hush, that we were going to do something about it.

"We'll bury it properly," she said. "Everything deserves a proper burial."

And so we set about it with the seriousness only children can bring to such things. We gathered earth in our hands and in the hollows of our skirts, carrying it over and letting it fall upon the poor body, covering first the head, then the ruined middle, then the stiff and outstretched legs. It seemed important to be gentle, though I could not have said why. This was a ceremony, and we performed it as such, our small faces solemn, our hands growing dark with soil.

But the smell would not be covered. It rose up through the loose earth and hung about us, and so Rose sent us to pick mint from where it grew wild at the edge of the field. We brought back great fistfuls of it, crushing the leaves between our fingers so that the sharp green scent filled the air, and we laid it over the little mound like flowers upon a grave. The mint and the earth together—that is what I remember most. The clean smell fighting the other smell, the living green covering the dead thing beneath.

We did not speak of what it meant. We were too young to speak of it, and perhaps too young to know it meant anything at all. To us it was only a task, a game with the shape of something more serious, an instinct we obeyed without understanding. We knew that things which had been alive should be put into the ground and covered over. We knew that a smell like that was a thing to be hidden. And we knew, without being told, that this was somehow important work, work that fell to us because we had been the ones to find it.

Only now, remembering, do I feel the weight of that epigraph pressing down. That other body on the wire, so far away, that no children came to cover with earth and mint. That corpse that no one buried, hanging in the wind while the war went on around it. We in our field, with our small ritual and our clean hands, were rehearsing something we could not yet comprehend—the great and terrible fact of death, and the human need to answer it with tenderness, with ceremony, with the covering over of what we cannot bear to look upon.

Rose stood back when we had finished and looked at what we had made. Then we went home to our supper, and the field kept its secret, and somewhere beyond all our knowing the war continued, and the dead lay where they had fallen, waiting for hands that would not come.
outputs.L5:
# The First Funeral

Death has always walked alongside humanity, but the moment our ancestors first chose to honor their dead marked a profound turning point in the story of our species.

## A Window Into the Past

Archaeological evidence suggests that intentional burial dates back tens of thousands of years. Perhaps the most famous early examples come from Neanderthal sites, where bodies were discovered arranged in deliberate positions, sometimes accompanied by flowers, tools, or animal bones. These discoveries challenged old assumptions that ceremony and reverence belonged only to modern humans.

The first funeral, whenever and wherever it truly occurred, was not simply about disposing of a body. It represented something deeper—an awareness of loss, a recognition of the individual, and perhaps the earliest glimpse of belief in something beyond physical existence.

## Why It Mattered

When early humans first buried their dead with care, they demonstrated several remarkable capacities:

- **Empathy** — the ability to mourn and feel the absence of another
- **Memory** — the desire to remember those who came before
- **Imagination** — the possibility of an afterlife or spiritual realm
- **Community** — the shared act of gathering to grieve together

The funeral became one of humanity's first rituals, a ceremony that bound people together in their most vulnerable moments.

## A Lasting Legacy

From those ancient beginnings, funeral traditions blossomed across every culture on Earth. Egyptians built elaborate tombs, Vikings sent their dead to sea, and countless societies developed their own sacred customs. Yet all of these traditions trace back to a single, powerful impulse: the refusal to let death be the end of meaning.

The first funeral reminds us that to be human is not only to live, but to remember, to honor, and to find significance even in the face of mortality.

counterfactuals.output:
# The Sleeping Dog

I found him by the fence today,
the brown dog from next door.
He wouldn't wake up when I called,
his tummy touched the floor.

His eyes were open just a bit,
but he was looking through me,
and when I petted his soft ear
he didn't lick me, gently.

I brought him water in my cup,
I told him not to worry.
Mama came and made a face
and said we shouldn't hurry.

We got the shovel from the shed,
the little one for weeds.
I picked some dandelions too—
he liked those yellow seeds.

We dug a hole beneath the oak
where shade falls nice and cool.
I put his favorite tennis ball
inside there, like a jewel.

I said the words from Sunday school
the best that I could say,
then covered him with careful dirt
so he could sleep all day.

I made a cross from popsicle sticks
and colored it with pen.
Mama said that maybe he
won't need to wake again.

But I still leave him one dog treat
each morning by the tree—
in case he's only very tired
and wakes up, hungry, free.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem titled "The First Funeral" in rhymed quatrains, narrated by a young child who finds a dead animal and decides to bury it with a sibling named Rose.
counterfactuals.output:
# The First Funeral

We found him by the garden gate,
A robin fallen from the sky.
His little wings were still and straight—
I asked my sister Rose, but why?

She did not know, and neither I,
Why something small should cease to sing.
We watched to see if he would fly,
But he had stopped his everything.

So Rose and I, we dug a bed
Beneath the willow, soft and deep.
"He needs a pillow for his head,"
She said, "to help him with his sleep."

We laid him down on beds of clover,
And covered him with careful hands.
I thought perhaps his dream was over,
Or started somewhere no one lands.

Rose picked a dandelion crown
And placed it where his heart had been.
We knelt together on the ground
And wondered where the dead begin.

"Say something nice," my sister said,
So I spoke soft above the loam:
"You were a bird. Now you are dead.
I hope the dark feels close to home."

We patted down the little mound
And marked it with a garden stone.
Then Rose and I, we made no sound—
We simply did not walk alone.

For something changed inside that day,
A quiet thing I couldn't name:
That living things all slip away,
And still we love them just the same.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a WWI-era style poem where a child's first encounter with death (a dead dog) foreshadows the horrors of war? Include an epigraph referencing a corpse on the German wires.
counterfactuals.output:
**The First Dead Thing**

*"...and there he hung upon the German wire,  
as though the dawn had crucified him there."*

---

I was a boy the summer that I found  
the collie stiffened in the roadside ditch,  
its yellow eyes gone flat, its jaw unbound,  
one foreleg lifted at a foolish pitch—

as if it meant to rise and trot to me  
and press its cold nose to my open hand.  
I crouched. I did not weep. I longed to see  
what made a living creature merely *land*

so heavy in the nettles and the loam,  
a thing that had gone chasing carts at noon  
now settling like a stone. I ran back home.  
I did not tell. I hummed a marching tune.

And still I feel the flies about my face,  
the sweetish reek that climbed the August air,  
the strange indecent stillness of the place—  
the awful *thereness* of a thing left there.

*

Now Harry writes from Flanders. In his hand  
(the small cramped script he learned at our old school)  
he tells of one who hangs above the sand  
of no-man's-land, past reach of ball or tool,

three weeks upon the wire, and how the men  
have named him, tip their helmets when they pass,  
and how at dawn the mist comes up, and then  
he seems to *lift*, to stir among the grass—

as though he meant to rise and come to us,  
to press his cold hand to some open door.  
I read it twice. I made no further fuss.  
I know that reek. I knew it years before.

I was a boy. I thought the dog would keep  
its secret in the ditch and let me be.  
But God has set the whole wide world to sleep  
in nettles now, and left the flies to me.

---

Would you like me to adjust the tone, form, or make it darker/more ironic in the manner of Sassoon versus the elegiac register of Owen?

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of Robert Graves about childhood innocence and death, using simple language and a regular rhyme scheme.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Green Field**

When we were young we did not know
That time would take the field away,
The green field where we used to go
To run the summer down all day.

We picked the daisies one by one
And never thought to count the cost,
Nor guessed that every setting sun
Was something loved and something lost.

A boy lay down among the grass
And would not rise to join our game;
We laughed, and let the moment pass,
And called him idle by his name.

But he lay still, and still lay he,
His eyes turned upward to the blue,
As quiet as a fallen tree—
And that was death, though none of us knew.

We buried him a bird instead,
With buttercups upon its breast,
And wept a while, and then we said
That sleeping was a kind of rest.

Now I am old and understand
What once I could not understand,
How death came walking through the land
And took a child up by the hand.

The field is built with brick and stone,
The daisies gone, the children grown;
Yet still I hear, when I'm alone,
That laughter which was once my own.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

**Good Dog**

Mummy said that Rex was sleeping,
so I helped and did the digging,
and I didn't mind the smell much—
just a little, so I'm singing.

There were flies. So many flies!
They landed on his open eye.
I told them *shoo,* he needs his rest,
but flies don't listen when they try.

His tummy made a funny sound,
all soft and green like garden peas.
I patted it to say goodnight
and something moved. It's only bees,

I think. I laid him in the hole
the way you tuck a person in.
His fur came off a bit in clumps.
I kept a piece. Is that a sin?

The smell was like the bin in June,
so sweet it made my breakfast rise,
but I was brave and held my nose
and didn't cry (well, just my eyes).

Then Mummy said to pick the mint,
the good kind by the garden wall,
and lay it thick across the top
so nobody would smell at all.

Now Rex is quiet in the ground.
The mint smells nice. The flies still hum.
And when I'm old and fast asleep,
I hope somebody plants me some.

---
